turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hello, Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you too. Well... I suppose I'm here because things at work have gotten really complicated lately. I work as a cashier—which, you know, I have a bachelor's degree, so it's not exactly where I thought I'd be at 54, but a job is a job, right? You have to pay the bills. But lately, well, I came in because when I'm standing at the register, I keep getting... stuck. I just get stuck doing these things that absolutely don't fit the moment. 

Like, I'll be ringing someone's groceries up, and instead of just sliding the can of soup or whatever across the glass, I start tapping the scanner. And it's not just a random tap, I have to tap it in this specific pattern, and I just keep doing it instead of scanning. Or, even worse, it happens when I'm making change. The register drawer will pop open, and I'll reach down to grab the fives or the ones, and my hand just stops. It completely freezes right over the cash drawer. I'll just be standing there, completely still, hovering over the money, and the customer is just standing there staring at me, waiting for their change. You know how people get at the store, they start shifting their weight, sighing, clearing their throats because they're in a hurry... and I know they're waiting, but I just stay frozen there. 

It's been causing a lot of problems, obviously, because the lines get backed up. And, well, last week it finally got me written up. My manager pulled me off the floor and took me into the back office and actually put a formal warning in my file about it. He said I was holding up the flow of the store, which I understand, but I just can't seem to stop getting stuck like that. So... I guess that's what brings me in.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes severe disturbances in motor control and behavior inappropriate to the situation, such as repetitively tapping a scanner in a pattern and freezing completely still over a cash drawer.

turns.doctor_question: When you find yourself tapping the scanner or freezing over the cash drawer, do you feel an internal urge or a sense of 'must' that you are trying to satisfy, or does it feel more like your body is simply not obeying your commands?
turns.patient_response:
Well, that's the thing, Dr. Smith, it's not like an itch I have to scratch, if that makes sense. It's not like I'm standing there thinking, "Oh, I really need to tap this scanner right now, I just have to do it." It's nothing like that at all. It's more like... well, like my body just decides to do its own thing, completely independent of what I actually want to be doing, which is scanning the soup and getting the customer out of my line. 

I'll be standing there, looking right at the can of soup, knowing exactly what I'm supposed to do, and my hand just starts doing the tapping pattern. Tap, tap, tap-tap. Just like that. And I'm in my head going, "What are we doing? Stop tapping, scan the soup," but my hand just keeps going. And the freezing, oh, the freezing is exactly the same. I'll see the five-dollar bill in the drawer, I'll know the customer needs five dollars and thirty-two cents in change, I reach down, and then... nothing. It's like the connection between my brain and my arm just gets severed right at the elbow. I'm telling my hand to grab the bill, I'm practically screaming at it in my head because I can hear the customer sighing and shifting their weight, but my hand just hovers there. It's completely stuck. 

It's so frustrating because I know it doesn't fit the moment. I know it's completely inappropriate for a cashier to just stand there frozen like a statue or tapping on the glass while a line of six people is waiting. And my manager, well, he doesn't understand it either, which is why he wrote me up last week. He thinks I'm just spacing out or not paying attention, but I am paying attention! I'm acutely aware of everything happening, I just can't make my body cooperate with the situation. So, no, it's not an urge at all. It's just... getting stuck, plain and simple.

turns.patient_response:

I can read the tiny print on the coupons people bring in—and let me tell you, people bring in these crumpled up, faded coupons from three months ago and expect me to honor them, so I have to read the expiration dates very carefully. If my vision was going bad, I'd definitely notice it there, but my eyes are doing just fine. 

And as for feeling confused or losing track of where I am... no, absolutely not. Never. That's actually the most maddening part of this whole situation with the register, Dr. Smith. I am completely, one hundred percent aware of my surroundings. I know exactly where I am—I know I'm at register four, I know it's Tuesday afternoon, I know the manager, Greg, is probably watching me from the front office window. I don't lose time, and I certainly don't get confused about what I'm doing. When my hand is hovering over that cash drawer, I know exactly what the money is, I know the math, I know who the change belongs to. I'm just trapped there watching it happen. If I were confused, well, maybe it wouldn't be so incredibly embarrassing, you know? If I was just lost in a daydream or forgot where I was, I could excuse it. But I'm not. I'm fully present, my mind is completely sharp. So, no, none of those things you mentioned. My head is clear, my eyes are fine, and I know exactly where I am at all times. It really is just this bizarre thing with my hands getting stuck.

Twenty cents! And she was getting quite loud and condescending about it. Now, if I were irritable or impulsive, or if I was losing my grip on how to behave socially, that would be the perfect time to snap, wouldn't it? To just tell her to pay the difference or leave the store. But I didn't do anything like that. I just smiled, apologized for the confusion, called Greg over to do a price override, and waited patiently. I didn't raise my voice, I didn't get angry. I followed all the customer service protocols to the letter, just like I always do. 

And as for social norms, well, I've always been a very polite, rule-following kind of guy. I have my bachelor's degree, I know how to conduct myself in a professional and public setting. I say 'please' and 'thank you,' I hold the door for people, I make polite small talk about the weather when I'm ringing up the groceries. I don't just blurt things out or act inappropriately. Even my sister, who calls me every single Sunday evening without fail, hasn't said a word about me acting differently. We just talk about her garden and my week, same as always. If I were acting strange or being short with her, she would be the first one to tell me, believe me, she never holds back. 

So, really, my personality is completely intact. My mood is fine, my temper is perfectly under control. It's just... like I said, it's just this incredibly frustrating thing with my body freezing up or tapping at the register. But inside? In my mind and my personality and the way I treat people? I'm exactly the same guy I was ten years ago.

turns.patient_response:
Well, let me think about that. Anxiety... distress... no. No, I really wouldn't say that I do. It’s not like a panic attack or anything of that sort, if that’s what you’re getting at. No, there’s no anxiety at all. It’s completely out of the blue. I’m just doing my job one second, completely at ease, and the next second my body just hits the brakes. turns.doctor_question: Has anyone in your immediate or extended family ever struggled with similar experiences, such as hearing voices or having their body move in ways they didn't intend?
turns.patient_response:
In my family? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, if they did, they certainly never breathed a word of it to me or anyone else, not even at the Thanksgiving table after a few glasses of wine. 

My family is... well, we're a very practical, very grounded bunch, I suppose you could say. My father, for instance, he worked in logistics for a regional shipping company for thirty-five years. He was a very by-the-numbers sort of man. He never heard anything that wasn't physically there in the room with him. If he heard a voice, it was because someone was standing right in front of his desk handing him a clipboard or a shipping manifest. And my mother, she taught middle school history for decades, so she was always extremely focused on facts and dates and reality. She passed away about ten years ago, but I can tell you she was sharp as a tack right up until the very end. She never once froze up or stared off into space, except maybe when she was trying to remember if she'd left the oven on, but that's just a normal thing people do, isn't it? 

Even if you look at my extended family—I have an uncle out in Ohio who used to sell insurance, and a couple of cousins I still exchange Christmas cards with every December—none of them have ever mentioned anything remotely like this. We just don't have this sort of... this sort of strangeness in our bloodline, as far as I know. Everyone just goes to work, does their jobs, pays their taxes, and goes to sleep. 

That's honestly a big part of why I'm so incredibly baffled by all of this! It’s like I’m the only one in the entire history of my family who has ever had to deal with invisible people critiquing their bagging skills while they're just trying to earn a paycheck. If my grandfather or my great-aunt had ever experienced something like their hands just stopping in mid-air for no earthly reason, I’m absolutely sure there would be some sort of family lore about it, you know? Some hushed whispers at family reunions or a cautionary tale passed down. But there’s just nothing. We are, historically speaking, boringly normal. So, no, I really don't have anything to give you on that front. I don't think there's any family connection here at all.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient mentions dealing with 'invisible people critiquing their bagging skills', confirming auditory hallucinations.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes their 'hands just stopping in mid-air for no earthly reason', confirming abnormal motor behavior.

turns.doctor_question: During these episodes where you freeze, have you ever found that your body remains in the position you were placed in, or that you can be moved by someone else like a mannequin?
turns.patient_response:
Like a mannequin? Well... I mean, I don't think so. Honestly, no one has ever stepped up and tried to just grab my arm and reposition me while it's happening. I mean, can you imagine a customer just reaching across the conveyor belt to move my arm? That would be a complete violation of personal space. 

But the freezing itself, and these other movements, they are exactly why I came in to see you in the first place. Because at the register, I just keep getting stuck doing things that absolutely do not fit the moment. It’s not just standing still. Sometimes I get stuck tapping the scanner in a pattern. Just... tap, tap, pause, tap, right on the glass where the laser comes out, over and over in this specific rhythm, completely ignoring the groceries piling up. Or, like I mentioned, the freezing—I'll just freeze completely solid with my hand hovering right over the open cash drawer. I'll have the customer's change literally inches from my fingers, and my hand just stops dead, and I'm stuck there while the customer is waiting and staring at me, probably wondering if I'm trying to steal their money or if I'm just incredibly rude. 

It's completely inappropriate for the middle of a transaction, and it's entirely out of my control. And the worst part, the absolute worst part, is that last week it actually got me written up. My manager, Brenda—who usually puts me on register four because I’m so reliable—pulled me into the back office next to the breakroom and handed me a formal written warning for 'unprofessional delays' and odd behavior on the floor. Fifty-four years old, a bachelor's degree, decades of perfect employment, and I'm getting written up because my hand decides to tap out a rhythm on a barcode scanner or freeze like a statue over a pile of five-dollar bills! So, no, nobody is posing me like a doll, but my body is certainly getting stuck doing things it has absolutely no business doing right in the middle of my shift.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient confirms experiencing severe motor disturbances, specifically freezing in place (stupor/posturing) and repetitively tapping in a specific rhythm (stereotypy) that are inappropriate to the situation and out of their control.

turns.doctor_question: I know you mentioned your family is very grounded, but has anyone in your family ever been diagnosed with schizophrenia, psychosis, or any condition involving a break from reality?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, definitely not. I mean, if you're asking for an official diagnosis of... well, of any of those things you just named, the answer is absolutely zero. I’ve actually been racking my brain about this lately, trying to trace back through the family tree, you know, just to see if maybe there was some great-uncle or a second cousin who was, I don't know, hidden away or had some sort of "nervous breakdown" back in the fifties that nobody talked about, but there is just nothing. 

My parents... well, like I was saying before, my dad with his shipping manifests and my mom with her history curriculums... they wouldn't even know what to do with a break from reality! Reality was their entire world. They were entirely focused on the tangible, the concrete, the day-to-day business of just living and working. And even if you look at the wider family, the relatives out in Ohio or my mother's side from upstate, none of them have ever spent a single day in a psychiatrist's office, at least not to my knowledge. I mean, I think my cousin Greg might have gone to marriage counseling back in the late nineties, but that was strictly about finances and his wife's spending habits, nothing whatsoever to do with losing touch with the world or anything like that. 

It’s actually terribly frustrating for me, to be quite honest, because if there was a history—if I could point to my grandfather and say, 'Oh, well, Grandpa Arthur used to hear invisible critics too'—then at least this whole ordeal would make some kind of logical, medical sense! I could just chalk it up to genetics and say, well, it's just my turn, I suppose. But I'm completely isolated in this. It's just me. Fifty-four years of a perfectly normal, grounded existence, and then suddenly this starts out of nowhere and I'm getting written up by Brenda. So, no, not a single diagnosis of anything remotely like that in my entire family tree.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient strongly implies they are experiencing auditory hallucinations by stating that if their grandfather 'used to hear invisible critics too', their current ordeal would make sense, but they are 'completely isolated in this'.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever lost consciousness or had a seizure, where you were completely unaware of what was happening around you?
turns.patient_response:
A seizure? Oh, goodness, no. No, nothing like that. I've never passed out or fainted or... or lost time, if that's what you mean. 

I know it probably sounds a bit confusing, because I was just telling you about how I freeze up at the cash register, and I suppose from the outside, to a customer or to Brenda, it might look like I'm just not there. Like the lights are on but nobody's home, so to speak. But I assure you, I am completely, painfully aware of every single thing happening around me when I get stuck like that. I don't lose consciousness at all. In fact, it's almost worse exactly because I am so aware of it. I can see the customer tapping their foot or sighing, I can hear the crinkle of the plastic bags at the end of the belt, I can hear the terrible soft rock they play on the overhead speakers—it's always the same tired playlist every single Tuesday—and I hear all of it. I'm just trapped there. But my mind? My mind is wide awake. 

I've never collapsed to the floor or started shaking or had any sort of fit. I mean, I still drive myself to work every single morning. I have a very reliable 2008 Honda Accord, and I've never once felt faint behind the wheel or anywhere else for that matter. If I were passing out or having seizures, I'm sure the DMV would have revoked my license by now, right? They're incredibly strict about that sort of thing, and rightfully so, because driving a two-ton machine when you might suddenly black out is just a recipe for disaster. 

So, no, definitely no seizures. I've never been completely unaware of my surroundings, and I've never lost consciousness unless you count just going to sleep in my own bed at the end of the day. It's just my body that stops cooperating, not my brain shutting off.

turns.doctor_question: When you are frozen in place at the register, if someone were to gently try to move your arm or change your posture, would it feel like your body stays in that new position, almost like you are made of wax?
turns.patient_response:
Doctor, I... well, I feel like we might be going in circles a little bit here, because isn't that essentially what you just asked me a few minutes ago? About being moved like a mannequin? Like I was saying, no one has ever actually tried to touch me or repose me when this happens. I mean, people just don't do that to a cashier at a grocery store, thank goodness. They just stare, or they clear their throats, but they don't reach out and try to bend my arms. 

But to get back to the real issue—and I know I’ve already told you this, but it’s the entire reason I made this appointment in the first place—is that I keep getting stuck doing these things that completely do not fit the moment. It’s the tapping. The tap, tap, pause, tap on the scanner glass, or just... freezing entirely with my hand hovering in mid-air right over the open cash drawer. The customer is right there, waiting for their change, and I'm just stuck, unable to finish the transaction. That is what’s actually happening to me. 

It's not about being made of wax or someone molding my arms, it's about my body getting locked into these completely inappropriate behaviors right in the middle of my shift. And like I mentioned, it’s serious enough that Brenda wrote me up for it last week. That formal warning is sitting in my personnel file right now because of this freezing and tapping, not because anyone is trying to bend my arms around. So, I really couldn't tell you what it feels like to be moved, because no one has tried, but being stuck... that part is very, very real, and it's what I desperately need help with.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient confirms experiencing abnormal motor behaviors, specifically freezing in place (stupor) and repetitive tapping (stereotypy) during inappropriate moments at work.

turns.doctor_question: Since these symptoms began three months ago, have you had any medical tests, such as a brain scan or an MRI, to look for a physical cause for these episodes?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no. No brain scans, no MRIs, no... no CT scans or anything like that. I haven't seen a neurologist or had anyone put me in one of those big tubes. 

To be completely honest with you, up until I sat down in this chair today, I haven't seen any doctors at all about this. I know that probably sounds incredibly foolish, especially for someone my age. You hit fifty and suddenly every little ache and pain is supposed to be checked out, right? But you have to understand, when this all started about three months ago, it was so... so subtle at first. I just thought I was tired. Or stressed! The grocery store was short-staffed, Brenda was on everyone's case about scanning metrics, and I thought, well, of course I'm freezing up a bit, I'm just overworked. I thought maybe I wasn't sleeping well, or maybe my blood sugar was dropping because I usually only have a piece of toast and a cup of black coffee for breakfast before my shift. 

So I didn't rush out to get a brain scan. I tried eating a banana on my break. I tried going to bed at 9:30 instead of 10:30. I tried all these little, practical things because the idea that there was something physically, fundamentally wrong with my brain... well, that was just too terrifying to entertain. And then, of course, the freezing got worse, and the tapping started, and the voices—the invisible critics, as I call them—got louder, and suddenly I'm getting a formal write-up. That's when I realized a banana wasn't going to fix this. 

But even then, my first thought wasn't "I need an MRI." My first thought was, "I am losing my mind and I need a psychiatrist." So here I am. But no, to answer your question directly, I haven't had any sort of medical imaging or physical tests done. Just... just my own mounting panic over the last ninety days, trying to figure out how to keep my job while my brain decides to hit the pause button on me. Do you... do you think I need one? A brain scan, I mean? Is that something you think could be causing all of this?

turns.doctor_question: When you are at home, have you noticed any changes in your handwriting, such as it becoming smaller, shakier, or more difficult to control than it used to be?
turns.patient_response:
Handwriting? Gosh, I... I really don't think so. I mean, to be completely fair, I don't do nearly as much writing by hand as I used to. Back when I was getting my bachelor's degree—which feels like an absolute lifetime ago now, honestly—I used to fill up notebook after notebook with lecture notes. My hand would cramp up so badly by the end of a long seminar. But these days? The most writing I do at home is just... well, making out my grocery lists, or writing checks for the monthly bills. 

I still write physical checks, you know. I know everyone does everything online now, with the auto-pay and the apps, but I just feel so much better having a physical paper trail. So every second Tuesday of the month, I sit down at my little kitchen table with my checkbook and a good blue ballpoint pen—it has to be blue ink, I just strongly prefer it over black for some reason—and I write out the check for my rent, the electric bill, the water. And my signature... well, it looks exactly the same as it did twenty years ago. It’s always been a little bit of a hurried scrawl, just my natural penmanship, but it hasn't gotten any smaller or... or shakier, like you asked. 

I can control the pen perfectly fine. In fact, just the other day I was writing out a birthday card for my sister—she lives out in Ohio now—and I wrote a whole paragraph inside the card. I didn't have any trouble keeping my words on the lines, and I didn't notice my hand trembling or anything like that. The letters were the exact same size they've always been. 

So, no, I haven't noticed any changes there at all. My handwriting is just about the only thing that feels completely normal lately, to be perfectly honest with you. It's just the freezing up at the register that's the problem, and those invisible critics I was telling you about before. But the writing itself? Sitting at my table with a pen? No, that's all perfectly fine. Why, is handwriting supposed to change? Does that happen to people who freeze up like I do?
